results.q: What happens when the output buffer is full while encoding?
answer: When the output buffer is full, `pb_write()` checks `count > 0 && stream->callback != NULL` and then verifies `stream->bytes_written + count < stream->bytes_written || stream->bytes_written + count > stream->max_size`. If that condition is true, it sets `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "stream full")` and returns, skipping the rest of the function.

This is handled in pb_write() (pb_encode.c:95): it checks `count > 0 && stream->callback != NULL`, and when that is true it checks `stream->bytes_written + count < stream->bytes_written || stream->bytes_written + count > stream->max_size` (line 97); if true it sets `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "stream full")` and returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "stream full")`; then it checks `!stream->callback(stream, buf, count)` (line 107); if true it sets `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` and returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")`; then it calls one of write_callback(), buf_write() through pb_ostream_s.callback — which one depends on the data at run time (line 107), so the rest of pb_write() is skipped.

buf_write() sets `pb_byte_t *dest = (pb_byte_t*)stream->state` (line 55); then it sets `stream->state = dest + count` (line 56); then it checks `buf != NULL` (line 64); if true it calls memcpy(); then it returns `true` (line 69).

results.q: What happens when the decoder needs more bytes than are left in the input?
answer: This is handled in pb_read() (pb_decode.c:103): it checks `stream->bytes_left < count`, and when that is true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")`, so the rest of pb_read() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: read_callback(), buf_read() — the previous values stay in place.

Consequence: pb_readbyte() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` (pb_decode.c:127); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping read_callback(), buf_read().
Consequence: pb_readbyte() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` (pb_decode.c:131); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early.
pb_read()'s caller pb_skip_varint() checks `!pb_read(stream, &byte, 1)` (pb_decode.c:261) and then returns `false`.

results.q: What happens when a decoded message is missing a required field?
answer: When a decoded message is missing a required field, `pb_decode_inner()` sets an error with the message "missing required field" and returns. This causes `pb_read()` to detect the error and may return early, skipping further callbacks or reads.

This is handled in pb_decode_inner() (pb_decode.c:1205): it checks `(req_field_count & 31) != 0`, and when that is true it checks `fields_seen.bitfield[req_field_count >> 5] != (allbits >> (uint_least8_t)(32 - (req_field_count & 31)))` (line 1207); if true it sets `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "missing required field")` and returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "missing required field")`.

Consequence: pb_read() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` (pb_decode.c:104); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping read_callback(), buf_read().
Consequence: pb_read() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` (pb_decode.c:108); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early.

results.q: What happens when a varint is too long?
answer: When a varint exceeds the maximum length, `pb_decode_varint()` detects it at line 244, sets the error message to "varint overflow" via `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "varint overflow")`, and returns that error. The caller `pb_decode_svarint()` then sees the failure and returns `false`, propagating the error up the call chain.

This is decided in pb_decode_varint() (pb_decode.c:241): it checks `!pb_readbyte(stream, &byte)`; when that is NOT true it checks `bitpos >= 63 && (byte & 0xFE) != 0` (line 244); if true it sets `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "varint overflow")` and returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "varint overflow")`; then it sets `result |= (uint64_t)(byte & 0x7F) << bitpos` (line 247); then it sets `bitpos = (uint_fast8_t)(bitpos + 7)` (line 248).

Consequence: pb_read() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` (pb_decode.c:104); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping read_callback(), buf_read().
Consequence: pb_read() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` (pb_decode.c:108); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early.
pb_decode_varint()'s caller pb_decode_svarint() checks `!pb_decode_varint(stream, &value)` (pb_decode.c:1415) and then returns `false`.
pb_decode_svarint()'s caller pb_dec_varint() checks `!pb_decode_svarint(stream, &svalue)` (pb_decode.c:1514) and then returns `false`.

results.q: What happens when a field arrives with the wrong wire type?
answer: When a field arrives with the wrong wire type, `decode_basic_field()` immediately returns an error via `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "wrong wire type")`, skipping the rest of its logic. Consequently, the field’s previous value remains unchanged, and later `pb_read()` may also return early due to its own error checks. Other parts of the code also reject such bad input, but the primary effect is the early error return and no update to the field.

Invalid data is caught in decode_basic_field() (pb_decode.c:431): it checks `wire_type != PB_WT_VARINT && wire_type != PB_WT_PACKED`, and when that is true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "wrong wire type")`, so the rest of decode_basic_field() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: pb_dec_bool(), pb_dec_varint(), pb_decode_fixed32(), pb_decode_fixed64() — the previous values stay in place.

Consequence: pb_read() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` (pb_decode.c:104); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping read_callback(), buf_read().
Consequence: pb_read() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` (pb_decode.c:108); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early.

Bad input is also rejected in other places: decode_callback_field() rejects it when `wire_type == PB_WT_STRING` (pb_decode.c:799), reporting `*(pb_size_t*)field->pSize = field->tag`; decode_static_field() rejects it when `wire_type == PB_WT_STRING && PB_LTYPE(field->type) <= PB_LTYPE_LAST_PACKABLE` (pb_decode.c:510); pb_message_set_to_defaults() rejects it when `!(!decode_field(&defstream, wire_type, iter))` (pb_decode.c:1031), reporting `*(bool*)iter->pSize = false`.

results.q: What happens when messages are nested too deeply?
answer: When a nested message exceeds the allowed depth, `pb_make_string_substream()` records the size, adjusts the parent stream’s `bytes_left`, and returns `true`, causing the caller to return `false`. This triggers early exits in `pb_read()` and `pb_readbyte()`, skipping their callbacks and reads.

This is decided in pb_make_string_substream() (pb_decode.c:393): it checks `substream->bytes_left < size`; when that is NOT true it records it (`substream->bytes_left = (size_t)size`, `stream->bytes_left -= (size_t)size`) and returns `true`, so the rest of pb_make_string_substream() is skipped.
Consequence: pb_read() checks `stream->bytes_left < count` (pb_decode.c:103); `stream->bytes_left < count` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping read_callback(), buf_read().
Consequence: pb_readbyte() checks `stream->bytes_left == 0` (pb_decode.c:126); `stream->bytes_left == 0` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping read_callback(), buf_read().
pb_make_string_substream()'s caller decode_static_field() checks `!pb_make_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (pb_decode.c:519) and then returns `false`.
pb_make_string_substream()'s caller decode_callback_field() checks `!pb_make_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (pb_decode.c:804) and then returns `false`.
pb_make_string_substream()'s caller pb_decode_ex() checks `!pb_make_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (pb_decode.c:1230) and then returns `false`.
pb_make_string_substream()'s caller pb_dec_submessage() checks `!pb_make_string_substream(stream, &substream)` (pb_decode.c:1649) and then returns `false`.

results.q: What happens when an array has more items than its maximum size during encoding?
answer: When an array has more items than its maximum size during encoding, the function `encode_array()` checks `PB_ATYPE(field->type) != PB_ATYPE_POINTER && count > field->array_size` and, if true, returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "array max size exceeded")`, skipping the rest of the function. The earlier values in the stream remain unchanged because the subsequent calls to `pb_encode_tag()`, `pb_enc_varint()`, `pb_encode_varint()`, and `pb_write()` are not executed.

This is handled in encode_array() (pb_encode.c:150): it checks `PB_ATYPE(field->type) != PB_ATYPE_POINTER && count > field->array_size`, and when that is true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "array max size exceeded")`, so the rest of encode_array() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: pb_encode_tag(), pb_enc_varint(), pb_encode_varint(), pb_write() — the previous values stay in place.

results.q: What happens when the decoder reads a tag of zero?
answer: When the decoder reads a tag of zero, `pb_decode_inner()` checks `flags & PB_DECODE_NULLTERMINATED`; if that is NOT true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "zero tag")`, so the rest of `pb_decode_inner()` is skipped. Consequently, functions like `pb_field_iter_find()`, `pb_field_iter_find_extension()`, `decode_extension()`, and `pb_skip_field()` are not executed, leaving previous values unchanged. After this early return, `pb_read()` may then check `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` or `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")`, which depend on runtime values and may cause further early returns, skipping `read_callback()` and `buf_read()`.

This is decided in pb_decode_inner() (pb_decode.c:1090): it checks `flags & PB_DECODE_NULLTERMINATED`; when that is NOT true it returns through `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "zero tag")`, so the rest of pb_decode_inner() is skipped.
Because it returns early, these do not happen in this case: pb_field_iter_find(), pb_field_iter_find_extension(), decode_extension(), pb_skip_field() — the previous values stay in place.

Consequence: pb_read() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` (pb_decode.c:104); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "end-of-stream")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early, skipping read_callback(), buf_read().
Consequence: pb_read() checks `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` (pb_decode.c:108); `PB_RETURN_ERROR(stream, "io error")` depends on runtime values, so it may return early.

`pb_read` is called from within the decoding functions in `pb_decode.c`. It is invoked by `pb_decode()` (lines 93 and 99), by `pb_skip_varint()`, `pb_skip_string()`, `pb_skip_field()`, `read_raw_value()`, `pb_close_string_substream()`, `pb_decode_fixed32()`, `pb_decode_fixed64()`, `pb_dec_bytes()`, `pb_dec_string()`, and `pb_dec_fixed_length_bytes()`. The overall call chain starts at `main() → listdir() → pb_decode_ex() → pb_close_string_substream() → pb_read()`.

It is called by pb_read() at pb_decode.c:93, only when `count == 0` is false, only when `buf == NULL && stream->callback != buf_read` is true, repeatedly inside `while (count > 16)`; pb_read() at pb_decode.c:99, only when `count == 0` is false, only when `buf == NULL && stream->callback != buf_read` is true; pb_skip_varint() at pb_decode.c:261, repeatedly inside `do-while`; pb_skip_string() at pb_decode.c:278, only when `!pb_decode_varint32(stream, &length)` is false, only when `(size_t)length != length` is false. It is also called by pb_skip_field() (pb_decode.c:326), pb_skip_field() (pb_decode.c:328), read_raw_value() (pb_decode.c:354), read_raw_value() (pb_decode.c:361), read_raw_value() (pb_decode.c:365), pb_close_string_substream() (pb_decode.c:410), pb_decode_fixed32() (pb_decode.c:1433), pb_decode_fixed64() (pb_decode.c:1456), pb_dec_bytes() (pb_decode.c:1590), pb_dec_string() (pb_decode.c:1632), pb_dec_fixed_length_bytes() (pb_decode.c:1715). The full chain from the program's start is: main() → listdir() → pb_decode_ex() → pb_close_string_substream() → pb_read().

`pb_ostream_s.bytes_written` is updated in `pb_ostream_from_buffer()` (sets it to 0), in `pb_write()` (adds `count`), and in `pb_encode_submessage()` (sets a substream to 0 and later adds the substream’s `bytes_written`).
pb_ostream_s.bytes_written is a field of type `size_t`, defined in pb_encode.h:51 — the code describes it as: "Number of bytes written so far.".

It is set by pb_ostream_from_buffer() (`stream.bytes_written = 0`, line 86); pb_write() (`stream->bytes_written += count`, line 112); pb_encode_submessage() (`substream.bytes_written = 0`, line 768); pb_encode_submessage() (`stream->bytes_written += substream.bytes_written`, line 775).
It is read by main() (line 32), pb_write() (line 97), encode_array() (line 180), pb_get_encoded_size() (line 573), pb_encode_submessage() (line 750).
Following where its value goes: pb_ostream_s.bytes_written → pb_encode_submessage() → pb_write() → write_callback() → send() — so it ultimately influences send(), which is an output (socket send).

In short: pb_ostream_s.bytes_written carries a value produced by pb_encode_submessage(), pb_ostream_from_buffer(), pb_write() and consumed by encode_array(), main(), pb_encode_submessage(), feeding send(). pb_encode_submessage(), pb_write() both reads and updates it, so it also keeps state between calls.

results.q: Where is the stream error message errmsg set?
answer: The stream’s `errmsg` field is set in `pb_encode_submessage()` (lines 745 and 778) and cleared in `pb_decode_tag()` (line 308).
It is set in pb_message_set_to_defaults():
pb_message_set_to_defaults() (pb_decode.c:1009).

Step by step, it sets `pb_wire_type_t wire_type = PB_WT_VARINT` (line 1013); then it checks `iter->descriptor->default_value` (line 1016); if true it calls pb_istream_from_buffer() and sets `defstream = pb_istream_from_buffer(iter->descriptor->default_value, (size_t)-1)`; then it checks `!pb_decode_tag(&defstream, &wire_type, &tag, &eof)` (line 1019); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it repeats while `pb_field_iter_next(iter)` (line 1023); then it checks `!pb_field_set_to_default(iter)` (line 1025); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it checks `tag != 0 && iter->tag == tag` (line 1028); then it checks `!decode_field(&defstream, wire_type, iter)` (line 1031); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it checks `!pb_decode_tag(&defstream, &wire_type, &tag, &eof)` (line 1033); if true it returns `false` straight away; then it checks `iter->pSize` (line 1036); if true it sets `*(bool*)iter->pSize = false`; then it calls pb_field_iter_next(iter) (line 1039); ….

Related values are also set here: `stream->errmsg = substream.errmsg` in pb_encode_submessage() (pb_encode.c:745); `iter->message = message` in pb_field_iter_begin() (pb_common.c:161); `iter->submessage_index = 0` in advance_iterator() (pb_common.c:131); `iter->submessage_index = (pb_size_t)(iter->submessage_index + PB_LTYPE_IS_SUBMSG(prev_type))` in advance_iterator() (pb_common.c:152); `stream->errmsg = substream.errmsg` in pb_encode_submessage() (pb_encode.c:778); `stream->errmsg = NULL` in pb_decode_tag() (pb_decode.c:308).
The value is computed just before: `pb_type_t prev_type = (prev_descriptor >> 8) & 0xFF` (pb_common.c:143).
